items.title: Caos in Polonia. Tusk: 'Il partito PiS vuole distruggere la democrazia'
items.summary: Scontro con il presidente sovranista Nawrocki sulla Corte. Le destre sfidano il premier
items.content:
Le immagini del presidente della Repubblica Karol Nawrocki, che si fa largo tra la folla e tra gli agenti assieme ai suoi bodyguard per forzare l'ingresso nel palazzo della Corte Costituzionale, potrebbero restare a lungo nella memoria dei polacchi. Ma sono, certamente, il simbolo di uno scontro istituzionale senza precedenti, da tempo in atto ma ora emerso in tutta la sua drammaticità. E' lo scontro tra il sovranista Nawrocki e l'europeista Donald Tusk.

La Commissione europea ha invitato il presidente polacco a convalidare la nomina di otto nuovi giudici, poco dopo le consultazioni da lui tenute con i rappresentanti dei partiti della maggioranza centrista e dell'opposizione nazionalista, volte a trovare una via d'uscita dall'attuale crisi politica e istituzionale. "Spetta alle autorità polacche garantire che il Tribunale costituzionale possa funzionare in conformità con la Costituzione polacca e nel rispetto della giurisprudenza pertinente della Corte di giustizia dell'Ue", ha dichiarato all'Afp un portavoce della Commissione europea. "La nomina di otto nuovi membri del Tribunale costituzionale rientra nella competenza costituzionale del Sejm" (la camera bassa del parlamento), ha aggiunto, mentre il presidente polacco Karol Nawrocki si è rifiutato di ratificarla.

Tra una destra che, nonostante sia frammentata, in Polonia aspira a tornare a capo delle esecutivo alle elezioni del 2027 e la piattaforma moderata dell'ex presidente del Consiglio europeo, che al governo è stata ostacolata sin dall'inizio dal capo dello Stato. "L'attacco alla Corte è un'altra fase del processo di distruzione dello stato di diritto da parte del PiS. Uno Stato democratico deve essere capace di far rispettare la giustizia", è stato l'attacco di Tusk in serata, nel suo messaggio alla nazione.

Lo scontro ha come fulcro la Corte Costituzionale e la volontà di Tusk di nominare un nuovo gruppo di giudici, anche per andare incontro alla sentenza della Corte di Giustizia Ue, secondo la quale il tribunale di Varsavia "non è né indipendente né imparziale" a causa delle nomine dei togati del precedente governo guidato dalla destra di Mateusz Morawiecki. Ma i cinque giudici nominati dal governo Tusk, in questi mesi, non sono mai stati messi nelle condizioni di lavorare. Fino alla giornata di venerdì, quando il presidente della Corte Costituzionale Bogdan Swieczkowski, ex viceministro del PiS e nominato dal precedente esecutivo, è stato sospeso. Le forze di polizia hanno presidiato il palazzo del Tribunale, negando l'accesso a Swieczkowski. A quel punto, centinaia di manifestanti hanno cominciato a circondare la Corte Costituzionale. Ad aizzarli i leader della galassia delle destre polacche, a cominciare dal fondatore del PiS, il 77enne Jaroslaw Kaczyński, anche lui in piazza. Il vero colpo di scena si è avuto però in serata quando Nawrocki, in volo verso il Senegal, ha deciso di far rientro a Varsavia, unendosi alla testa dei manifestanti e accusando di fatto Tusk di "violazione dell'ordine costituzionale".

Nella giornata di sabato lo scontro non si è placato. Nawrocki ha tenuto consultazioni urgenti con i gruppi del Parlamento polacco mentre la giudice Anna Korwin-Piotrowska - che ha notificato la sospensione di Swieczkowski - ha emanato le prime direttive per permettere ai togati, inclusi i neonominati, di svolgere le proprie funzioni al di fuori della sede del tribunale. In serata a parlare è stato Tusk. Il premier ha puntato il dito direttamente contro Narowki - "un politico non può entrare in tribunale per emettere ordini o intimidire i giudici, anche se è presidente" - e ha assicurato che, sulla questione, non scenderà a compromessi. "Ieri abbiamo assistito a eventi scandalosi. Vorrei tanto che non si vedessero queste scene in Polonia, ma la via per la calma non può essere cedere all'illegalità o alla violenza", ha sottolineato. Per la Polonia, tuttavia, si prevedono giorni di caos. Lo scontro ha inoltre riunito i vari partiti di una destra che, in Polonia, negli ultimi mesi si è andata frammentandosi. Al PiS, ora fanno compagnia la nuova formazione del fuoriuscito Morawiecki (Sviluppo Più) e Konfederacja, la coalizione della destre più radicali, in forte ascesa. Tutti, però, hanno accusato Tusk di un tentativo di golpe annunciando una dura battaglia in Parlamento per sfiduciarlo. Il clima, da qui alle prossime elezioni previste in autunno, rischia di diventare drammatico. E la sua portata supera i confini della Polonia. Fratelli d'Italia (che al Pe è nello stesso gruppo del PiS), Lega e Patrioti si sono immediatamente schierati contro Tusk, puntando il dito contro il silenzio dell'Ue, che finora sullo scontro ha evitato di esporsi, al pari del Ppe. Perfino l'ambasciatore americano a Varsavia Tom Rose è entrato in campo chiedendo a tutti di non fomentare l'escalation. Non è rimasto a guardare neanche Lech Walesa, lo storico leader di Solidarnosc. "Primo Ministro Tusk, non abbiamo scelta. La nostra patria ha bisogno di aiuto! Sono al tuo fianco in prima fila", sono state le sue, chiarissime, parole.

items.title: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
items.summary: Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, has been stranded in the Cook Islands since 2023 and wants to return to Sri Lanka.
items.content:
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.

The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".

After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.

Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.

Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.

"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.

"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."

Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.

Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.

In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.

She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.

But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.

That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.

So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.

She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.

Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".

"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."

But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.

Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.

In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.

Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.

"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.

On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.

She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.

One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.

"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.

Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.

"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.

She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.

The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.

McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.

New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.

To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."

Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says

Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".

When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.

Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".

Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."

"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."

Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna Khan

If you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line . Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide , external .

items.title: Il Milan rinasce nel derby con show di Moreira, Inter vede le streghe
items.summary: La cronaca e le foto
items.content:
Il derby della notte delle streghe va al Diavolo. La risposta più rumorosa a chi lo aveva già messo in discussione, con i fischi dopo il ko con il Bologna. Il 3-1 si trasforma nel risultato perfetto per restituire entusiasmo ad Amorim, confermato a gran voce dal patron Cardinale ("è il mio coach, sono contento della scelta") che spoilera con una sciarada anche l'arrivo imminente di Markus Krösche come nuovo Head Of Football: non una vittoria casuale, non un successo costruito su un episodio fortunato, ma una serata di personalità, intensità e concretezza. E il giusto cinismo: Pulisic, Rabiot e Moreira segnano infatti nelle prime tre conclusioni nello specchio.

Una spia preoccupante invece per l'Inter, sotto 0-2 per la quinta volta stagionale, che non riesce a trovare tranquillità tra i pali: con Provedel out per un attacco influenzale, Martinez non dà mai la sensazione di essere realmente affidabile. Non ha colpe macroscopiche come nelle papere con il Real Madrid e il Club Brugge, ma non riesce a fare le parate che mutano il corso di una gara: lo scavetto di Rabiot (10') e la pennellata di Moreira (43') sono virtuosismi balistici su cui Martinez, per una cattiva posizione o poca reattività, non mette una pezza. Quello che invece riesce a far Maignan: il capitano rossonero non può fare nulla sul colpo di testa di Bastoni (22') e riscatta l'espulsione di Bournemouth con un autentico miracolo su Spence (34'), negandogli il 2-2 con un riflesso prodigioso dopo un tiro ravvicinato a botta sicura, per di più sporcato da Diawara. E trasuda sicurezza nelle uscite alte sui cross con cui l'Inter bombarda l'area rossonera. Ridurre la sconfitta alla differenza tra i due portieri sarebbe però ingeneroso.

Anche se l'Inter tira in porta il doppio delle volte (8-4). Il Milan già dopo 4', con il sigillo di Pulisic, mette in chiaro le cose: sarà una gara seria, di coesione, di sacrificio. Per Capitan America il modo migliore per festeggiare il rinnovo fino al 2031. Chivu si espone alle critiche per una formazione inedita e un modulo fluido: lascia in panchina l'affaticato Dimarco ma invece che confermare Esposito o schierare Bonny al posto dell'infortunato Lautaro opta per Diouf nella novella posizione di sottopunta con Susic a fare spola tra centrocampo e attacco. È un esperimento che non porta dividendi. Anzi, concede il dubbio che un undici più prudente dia maggiore coraggio alla squadra di Amorim, arrivata al derby con molto più da perdere, frutto della paura di poter scivolare a -10.

Ora, invece, si trova a -4 e la Lazio ha l'occasione di salire in vetta solitaria. Musah domina il confronto con Barella, lezioso e responsabile di regalare la punizione del 3-1. Rabiot non ha invece rivali, senza un vero filtro di protezione alle sue folate. Moreira asfalta Carlos Augusto: oltre al gol, anche due assist. Non convincono nemmeno i cambi del tecnico campione d'Italia: Esposito e Bonny in campo solo a una manciata di minuti dalla fine, in un arrembaggio tardivo. Ultima situazione degna di nota, la topica di Guida nell'assegnare un rigore all'Inter per un fallo di mano di Gila (75'). In realtà la palla finisce sul petto e il Var cancella la svista. Il Milan vince e rinasce, sorride Kakà - dopo aver pianto durante la cerimonia con cui è stato inserito nella Hall of Fame -, San Siro trema di gioia. Per Chivu il Milan resta indigesto: terza sconfitta su tre da quando è allenatore dell'Inter.

items.title: F1: Hamilton in pole, al suo fianco Russel. Antonelli parte quarto
items.summary: In prima fila anche la Mercedes
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton ha regalato alla Ferrari la pole position del GP del Messico di F1. Con lui partirà in prima fila la Mercedes di George Russell. Entrambi i piloti che ancora possono negare il titolo a Kimi Antonelli partiranno dunque davanti all'italiano, che scatterà in seconda fila, dietro Charles Leclerc. Max Verstappen era giunto quarto in qualifica, ma ha perso una posizione per la penalità dopo l'incidente nella FP2 di ieri con Lawson. La prima 'finestra' si é chiusa senza portare ad Antonelli il meritato titolo mondiale, ma quello di Austin era poco più di uno spiraglio, tante le combinazioni a lui favorevoli che si sarebbero dovute allineare.

A Città del Messico, anche grazie alla splendida vittoria ottenuta dal bolognese in Texas, il piatto della bilancia pende molto di più a suo favore. Il vantaggio del pilota Mercedes è di 123 punti sul compagno di squadra Russell a cinque gare dalla fine della stagione. L'inglese ed il suo connazionale Hamilton (-124) sono, come una settimana fa, gli ultimi irriducibili ancora in grado di insidiarlo. Ad Antonelli basterà il nono posto, o anche il decimo purché Russell non vinca; può anche non fare punti, purché né Russell né Hamilton vincano. Quest'ultimo ha cambiato il motore della sua SF-26, ma non é incappato in penalità perché si tratta di un propulsore già impiegato in passato. Kimi, superata l'influenza, ha ottenuto il secondo tempo al termine delle terze libere, preceduto di appena un millesimo da Norris. E' stata una sessione che ha reso ogni pronostico complicato perché in molti si sono alternati in vetta, con gomme medie fino a 10' dalla fine. A cominciare dallo stesso Antonelli, seguito dalle Ferrari di Hamilton e Leclerc e dalla W17 di Russell. Montate le soft, Antonelli ha ripreso il comando delle operazioni, superato solo dal guizzo del campione del mondo. La notizia che la Haas ha appiedato Esteban Ocon ha lasciato il paddock interdetto. Anche perché il team statunitense non ha dato spiegazioni della improvvisa decisione, precisando solo che il 30enne francese non ha problemi di salute. Secondo indiscrezioni, alla base dell'esclusione ci sarebbe un alterco con il team principal Ayo Komatsu, ieri sera, al termine delle libere 2. Ocon sarà sostituito dalla riserva, il giapponese Ryo Hirakawa, 32 anni, due volte campione del mondo endurance (2022, 2023) e vincitore della 24 Ore di Le Mans (2022) con Toyota. Ieri aveva preso parte alla FP1, facendo segnare il 15/o tempo. Domani farà il suo debutto in una gara di Formula 1 partendo dalla 19/a posizione.

items.title: Altoids Project
items.summary: Article URL: https://uvdn7.github.io/altoids-project/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50321048 Points: 82 # Comments: 4
items.content:
My 12-year-old son and I spent about two months on, what we call, the Altoids project. Here is the final product ( video ):

It all started when I took him to MIT Swapfest for the first time. We saw an assembled robot from a couple’s booth; later we learned that it was from a kit . It was built by their daughter many years ago. After realizing I had come with my son, they gave us the robot for free. We also picked up a used ThinkPad laptop at a very reasonable price, which we used for the project.

As any curious mind would, we disassembled the robot. Noticing that we were missing the control, we wanted to see which parts we could reuse. We took the 128x64 display off. But we couldn’t find the pinout for the display. We tried using AI, but it hallucinated so badly that it gave us a 20-pin pinout when the display only has 10 pins.

After hours of searching around, we found the exact schematic posted on Arduino’s forum by a stranger on the Internet. God bless him. With the pinout, we finally made the display show something. We ran the Space Trash game from the U8g2 library . Let’s call this v1.

I had just watched a YouTube video where someone built a tiny computer and fit everything inside an Altoids tin ( video ). Inspired by the YouTube video, we grabbed a random tin found in the house and moved the project to the workbench.

To reduce the form factor, we switched to an Arduino Nano , and ordered LiPo batteries and PowerBoost for power supply. Everything needed to fit in the tin. My son did all the CAD and 3D printing. Here is what v2 looked like. The lid did not close. It felt like playing 3D chess to fit everything in.

We ordered solderable breadboards to avoid the messy wires. It was looking promising. We also bought a real tin of Altoids from a grocery store, since the Altoids tin is actually a little taller than the one we were using earlier. This is what v3 looked like. The lid did not close, but we were getting closer.

The display was connected to a tiny solderable breadboard. We wanted to remove it and connect the wires to the display directly. But we had a really hard time with desoldering. We accidentally pulled one copper pad off the display, making it unusable. We might be possible to salvage it, but we just ordered a new display from Adafruit instead.

At this point, I wanted to avoid desoldering as much as possible. So we got those tiny hooks for testing the display ( video ). This is when we realized the new display does not default to SPI mode. We did not want to make more changes to the wiring, so we still had to desolder two jumpers.

I suspected our soldering iron was heating unevenly. We ordered a new soldering iron and it made all the difference. With the new iron, we made rapid progress. We hot-glued the display onto the lid. Everything worked for the first time. This is what v4 looked like. The lid did close with some struggle.

Two wires connecting the microcontroller and the display broke the next day. We did many hacks, one of which is to extend the wires by soldering two wires together. It did not work well, obviously. We got some ultra-fine (30 AWG) wires to replace them. At this point, my son did most of the desoldering and soldering work. He actually connected one wire incorrectly, so it did not work at first. It is a good debugging and learning experience.

As a final touch, we got tiny 1x1-inch ziploc bags and put two actual Altoids in the tin. And here we have the final product, after five iterations. None of the components used in the first iteration survived.

items.title: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/tree/main/examples/workflows/team-solve Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50320995 Points: 158 # Comments: 87
items.content:
A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ( below , every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files ( q38_multiagent_pN , fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read and $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p / top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included ( memdoor connect local for Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio or janis: how to connect one ).

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

Each step is one YAML file in steps/ , the format of mario , the engine underneath. requires: is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

items.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/italian-farmer-found-unknown-seeds-attic-with-nothing-lose-planted-them-result-biblical-180989644/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50320963 Points: 277 # Comments: 76
items.content:
Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them.

To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile.

“I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today?

Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says.

In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men-anticipating Jesus's "Feeding of the 5,000" in the gospels.

In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.

In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.

In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot-and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.

Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo —“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.”

Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets.

Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table.

Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent —the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field.

Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano , or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development.

In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl , during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain.

The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug , focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events.

In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting.

They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says.

One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli , a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special.

Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali , then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum —literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains.

The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago , an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more.

items.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
items.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
items.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.

All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.

The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.

The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".

On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.

The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.

Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

items.title: AI text watermarking and quality loss
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.keyvan.net/p/ai-text-watermarking-and-quality Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50320599 Points: 43 # Comments: 7
items.content:
After the EU AI Act’s transparency guidelines went into effect, and following the announcement that most major AI labs will soon be watermarking their text output to comply, there has been some debate about how much of an impact this is going to have, if any, on the quality of the text produced by AI models.

Since the focus of AI labs shifted to code production, I think the written output of the models has gotten much worse. 1 But it’s still interesting to try to understand if watermarking could make it even worse.

I found the discussion around technology writer John Gruber’s recent post, Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing , very interesting.

It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance.

He got a lot of pushback, with many debating how you would even measure quality, or define it.

But some argued that watermarking does not affect quality at all: it’s essentially just using different random numbers to generate the text. Daniel Jalkut, whom Gruber linked to in his follow-up, published a piece titled AI Can’t Adulterate its Own Writing , in which he wrote:

…there are also ways of tweaking the algorithm that would not diminish its randomness. For example if a random number generator routinely reversed the order of the digits in a generated number, the randomness would remain the same.

Similarly, in another discussion, someone described it as essentially swapping two faces of a die.

I hope that’s true. I believe it’s possible that it is true. I think it’s highly unlikely that it is true.

Anthropic make a bold claim: “ Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output. ” The paper they link to and based their design on (Google’s SynthID-Text, published in Nature in 2024) assures everyone that the method “ preserves response quality ”.

So it’s easy to assume there’s been a lot of fuss over nothing, that they really are just swapping some random numbers around.

But their no-quality-impact claim, which they tested with humans, is based on single responses. Not the way millions of people actually use these systems: as back-and-forth conversations, over time, over multiple prompts and responses.

The 56-page supplementary PDF they link to at the bottom provides some more info on the method used, and it suggests the no-quality-impact claim isn’t telling the full story. Notably, it says that there is a “diversity/detectability trade-off”:

While single-sequence non-distortion guarantees the quality of each individual response, it does not necessarily preserve diversity across multiple responses

when sampling several responses to the same prompt, the similarity between the responses is greater for the watermarked responses than the unwatermarked responses.

Now, if they had truly only swapped one set of random numbers for another, we would not be seeing any such difference compared to the unwatermarked responses.

This could be problematic in scenarios where inter-response diversity is important, or could lower the overall quality of a system which generates many responses then selects the best one

Okay, so in their own words, it can “lower overall quality” after all. But nothing to worry about, because this would only concern you if you cared about “inter-response diversity”, for which they only provide one example: a system which generates and selects responses.

But “inter-response diversity” affects how most people use these systems too. Especially for writing tasks where you want creativity.

In response to Gruber’s point about sacrificed quality, some argued that the model has no notion of the best next word to use for what each individual is trying to convey in their specific work, and so we shouldn’t get too hung up on the next word choice. But then surely they’d agree that you, the individual, would know if it’s suitable or not once you see it.

Let’s say you prompt: “I don’t like the ending to this sentence. Please suggest a new one: [sentence].” The model suggests an alternative, but you don’t like it. No problem, hit the retry button. Well, now you’re affected by watermarking, because you have hit the “inter-response diversity” problem: like throwing a loaded die, you’ll see similar responses more than you would with an unwatermarked model.

Natzir Turrado, a technical consultant, actually tested this (article in Spanish) by reproducing SynthID-Text on an open model with the paper's settings and a watermark key. He asked the watermarked model five times to describe a memorable trip to a coastal town. Four of the five answers he got back opened in a near-identical way: “My heart still sings/dances when I think back to my trip to the quaint coastal town of…”. For the unwatermarked model, three opened in different ways. 2

And though they don’t appear to have tested for it, the same thing that makes answers to the same prompt look similar could happen across different prompts too. The watermark only looks at a small sliding context window when choosing the next token, so any time two pieces of writing pass through the same short token sequence, they could be recreating the same context window, leading to a more predictable and less diverse output. And writing is full of identical short phrases that could trigger this behaviour.

Here’s another example of what this affects: one way people try to determine the confidence level of a response, to lower the chances of hallucinations, is to repeat the same prompt a number of times, to explore the different pathways the model takes. They then look at the results to see where the consensus lies. Well, this is also affected. With watermarking, you’re less able to trust the consensus you see forming, because the answers are now less independent: they’re steered by the watermark key.

What’s interesting is that while the SynthID paper points to the loss of quality across responses, I couldn’t find anywhere in the paper where they tested this particular aspect of the watermarking method with humans. If they didn’t, the wonderful human test results they point to did not involve testing the most affected part of the watermarking method. 3

So it seems to me that they are sacrificing quality, by limiting the creative range of their models through watermarking, and they don’t think you’ll notice or care much. 4

A pattern Jasmine Sun found looking at why AI models don't write well. Here’s what Katy Gero, a poet and computer scientist, had to say:

The same whimsicality that made GPT-2’s voice fresh also made it prone to other unpredictable behavior. “If you’re a big corporation like Google or OpenAI, you want a chatbot that’s going to make money. The chatbot that’s not going to make you money is the one that’s a weirdo,” Gero said.

Natzir Turrado pointed me to a reply he received on X from one of the SynthID paper’s authors, Sumanth Dathathri:

There's a lot of easy fixes to the diversity issue. I think if you tried the same prompt with Gemini/Claude many times , you'd get very diverse responses :)

It’s a bit ambiguous, but I wonder if his “easy fix” is shifting the problem to the user. It reads to me like he’s acknowledging that they’ve replaced the previous die with a loaded one, but the solution is just to roll it “many times” (my emphasis), and it’ll eventually land on each of its faces. If that is what he’s saying, why not admit that such a change does make the system worse than it was before for the user?

Turrado responded : “Curious: which easy fixes don’t trade off detection strength?”

A recent paper recognised that this is an “understudied fundamental trade-off in LLM watermarks: quality-diversity-power, i.e., the trade-off between the quality of the watermarked text, the output diversity under the watermarking scheme, and the overall watermarking signal strength.”

There are ways to mitigate some of the effects to make them less noticeable to an individual using a chat app, e.g. by rotating watermark keys between each of their requests. But these are not fixes. They only dilute the effect, and have their own costs, e.g. making watermarking less effective on shorter texts, and more costly to detect. As another study pointed out : “achieving a perfect distortion-free watermark is impossible”.

items.title: Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
items.summary: More than 320,000 people demonstrated across France against the rising cost of living and poor public services, with clashes between some protesters and police.
items.content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.

In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.

More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.

The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.

Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

items.title: Manovra, scontro sulla scuola. Banche ancora sotto tiro
items.summary: Il testo della legge di bilancio sotto il fuoco incrociato di opposizioni, sindacati ed enti locali. A fare polemica all'indomani della pubblicazione è soprattutto la stretta sugli organici della scuola
items.content:
Il taglio degli organici della scuola, proprio mentre gli studenti scendono in piazza. Le pensioni come riserva da cui attingere risorse. Il taglio alle tasse del ceto medio solo per un anno, a fronte di una flat tax che sale per gli autonomi. Le risorse insufficienti alla sanità, che mandano in allarme le Regioni.

Il testo della legge di bilancio è appena diventato pubblico ma è già finito sotto il fuoco incrociato di opposizioni, sindacati ed enti locali.

E mentre si avvicina l'avvio della sessione di bilancio, con un 'tesoretto' di 120 milioni per il 2027 per le modifiche parlamentari (altri 120 nel 2028), il vicepremier Matteo Salvini non allenta la pressione sulle banche, aprendo a possibili ulteriori interventi. Ma a fare polemica all'indomani della pubblicazione della manovra è soprattutto la stretta sugli organici della scuola . La legge di bilancio mette nero su bianco 4.925 posti in meno nelle dotazioni dell'autonomia scolastica e 2.049 posti nell'organico del personale Ata, per un totale di 6.974 unità. Un intervento che genera risparmi per quasi 252 milioni di euro all'anno a partire dal 2028. "Quando c'è da fare cassa, il governo sa sempre dove colpire: sulla scuola", va all'attacco il Pd. "Una vergogna assoluta", la bolla il M5s. Per Avs è "la finanziaria dei ricchi". E fa discutere anche la decisione di rivedere, visto il calo delle nascite, il riparto dei fondi per gli asili nido.

"Il governo non apre asili, aspetta che nascano meno bambini", commenta amara la responsabile scuola del Pd Irene Manzi. Ad alzare un muro contro i tagli alla scuola è anche la segretaria generale della Cisl Daniela Fumarola, che chiede al governo di aprire subito un confronto con il sindacato. "Di fronte al disagio delle nuove generazioni, alle povertà educative e alle crescenti difficoltà del lavoro scolastico, servono investimenti e personale, a partire da docenti e ATA e non certamente tagli", avverte. Si allarga invece a tutta la manovra il giudizio fortemente critico che arriva dalla Cgil. Con l'inflazione alle stelle, la perdita di potere d'acquisto dei salari, e l'emergenza costi dell'energia, la manovra "sembra scritta dal governo di un altro Paese, per non dire di un altro pianeta", commenta il sindacato di Maurizio Landini, che si prepara allo sciopero del 20 novembre: "Qui siamo al di là delle peggiori aspettative": "si accelerano declino e impoverimento".

Le tabelle della manovra quantificano anche la portata della nuova stretta in arrivo sulla rivalutazione delle pensioni: i tagli all'adeguamento all'inflazione, che resta pieno solo per gli assegni fino a 4 volte il minimo, si traducono in un risparmio per le casse dello stato di 14,2 miliardi in 10 anni (8,5 al netto degli effetti fiscali). "Per distribuire mance e finanziare la propaganda, il governo taglia sulla scuola e sulle pensioni", commenta il capogruppo Dem al Senato Francesco Boccia. Sulle polemiche scoppiate dopo i tagli sulla scuola interviene intanto il vicepremier Matteo Salvini, che difende i "miracoli" fatti in questi anni dal collega Valditara, ma apre comunque a modifiche: "se ci fossero delle variazioni e delle migliorie, il Parlamento è lì apposta". E proprio in sede di conversione potrebbe arrivare qualche nuova sorpresa per le banche, su cui il leader della Lega resta in pressing. "Se il Parlamento riterrà che si possa chiedere, fare, ottenere anche qualcosa in più, il Parlamento è sovrano", dice. Il vicepremier si mostra invece freddo sulla misura delle targhe personalizzate: "Se io devo pagare più soldi per avere la targa personalizzata, non li pago. Però questo è un parere mio". Altro tema che entrerà nel dibattito parlamentare è sicuramente quello della 'previdenza dedicata' per le forze dell'ordine. Dopo la tragedia che ha colpito i militari italiani in Bosnia, Per FI è "un imperativo morale battersi fino in fondo" per ottenerla, assicura il leader azzurro Antonio Tajani, che promette: "Faremo di tutto perché venga inserita già nell'articolato. Se necessario - promette - presenteremo un emendamento durante l'esame parlamentare".

items.title: Kakà in lacrime prima del derby: la standing ovation di San Siro commuove il fuoriclasse
items.summary: L’ex trequartista brasiliano, entrato nella Hall of Fame rossonera, piange commosso prima del fischio d’inizio di Milan-Inter
items.content:
San Siro rende omaggio all’ultimo Pallone d’Oro della Serie A (2007). Ricardo Kakà , prima del derby Milan-Inter , viene premiato in mezzo al campo per l’ingresso nella Hall of Fame rossonera . Standing ovation di tutti i tifosi di fede milanista, che partono con il vecchio coro: “Siam venuti fin qua, per vedere segnare Kakà”. Il trequartista brasiliano, di fronte a un tale tributo, non riesce a trattenere le lacrime e si commuove.

Kaka was in tears after receiving a standing ovation at the San Siro. He has been added into Milan's Hall of Fame. ❤️ https://t.co/uz0Ci48Jcu

Prima del fischio d’inizio ai microfoni di Sky sport Kakà ha detto: “Bellissimo essere qui, vedere una partita così con tutto questo affetto dei milanisti. Veramente ancora una serata speciale per me qua. Cardinale ha fatto un discorso molto bello del progetto per questo Milan, quindi tutti noi milanisti abbiamo molta fiducia che da qui in poi il Milan possa ritornare a essere protagonista sia in Italia che in Europa. Derby più bello? Per me quello del 3-2 è bellissimo, però anche quello di Champions, quarti di finale, penso che abbiamo vinto sia all'andata che al ritorno, quindi quello per me è molto speciale”.

items.title: Surviving "The Graduate"
items.summary: https://archive.ph/Eqn1F Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50319563 Points: 93 # Comments: 29
items.content:
When I went down to the pool at the Chateau Marmont, it seemed like everyone knew each other and was having fun in the sun.

I had been staying with my parents in L.A., shooting “The Graduate,” but my father was driving me crazy. Every day, I’d get home from the set, and he’d grill me, wanting to know every detail of what happened. And he’d be very critical: Why did you do that? That’s not the way to do it. I lasted maybe five days, and then I couldn’t take it anymore. I was trapped in the house where I’d grown up, totally alienated by the previous generation, just like my character. So I’d moved to the hotel where the cast and crew were staying.

Out by the pool, it was like a cabana party on Mount Olympus: the people looked like golden gods among the palm trees. I felt immediately uncomfortable, unworthy. Here I was, playing a starring role in a movie by Mike Nichols , who was the director of the moment, but I felt like I had no right to be there.

The shoot went on for months. Mike was in no rush; he had all the time and money he wanted. But I never went down to the pool again.

“The Graduate” exacerbated all my insecurities from the start. When my agent said that Mike was interested in me, I didn’t even want to try out for the part. I had read the Charles Webb novel that Mike was adapting, and it was obvious that I was all wrong for Benjamin. A track star and straight-A student, the head of the debate team—this was an affluent, all-American kid, whose surname was “Braddock.” Why would you cast a person who looks as ethnic as I do to play the ultimate Wasp? It made absolutely no sense.

It was impossible to be unimpressed by Mike, though. His first film, “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?,” had just been nominated for thirteen Academy Awards, including Best Directing and Best Picture. I’d enjoyed his version of “Barefoot in the Park” on Broadway, and I loved the comedy routines he’d done with Elaine May. Still—me, playing a six-foot gentile? I had to draw the line somewhere.

“I hear you don’t think you’re right for the part,” Mike said on the phone. “So who is right for it?”

There happened to be a copy of Time on the coffee table in front of me; on the cover was a sketch of a handsome, blond, athletic fellow meant to represent Americans “Twenty-five and Under.” “The guy on the cover of Time, ” I said.

“You’re saying you’re not right for it because you’re Jewish,” Mike said.

There was a pause. Then Mike said, “Maybe he’s Jewish inside .”

By that time, they’d been trying to cast the part for almost two years. “Robert Redford and Candice Bergen, the ideal couple—that’s what we were thinking,” Buck Henry, the film’s co-screenwriter, said about casting Benjamin and his love interest, Elaine. But they’d already seen Redford—and pretty much everyone else—by the time they got around to me and Katharine Ross. Nothing had clicked. I still maintain that if I’d read for them at the beginning of their search, instead of at the bitter end, I never would have got the part.

The irony is that I was just starting to become successful in theatre, the world I’d inhabited for almost a decade. I was in “Eh?” Off Broadway, and I was having a great experience: lots of laughs, standing ovations almost nightly, my face on the cover of the Arts section of the Times. I was finally making a living doing what I loved. It was as if I’d been hiking up a mountain and, just when I could finally see the summit, here comes Mike in a helicopter, offering me a ride to a different peak.

Hollywood had never been my endgame. As far as I was concerned, the studios kept beautiful people imprisoned in seven-year contracts. I wasn’t beautiful, and I didn’t want to be trapped. To be honest, I looked down on American movies, compared with theatre. When it came to breakthrough cinema, the kind made in Europe by greats like Truffaut, Buñuel, Antonioni, and Godard, Hollywood had yet to see the light.

My agent convinced me that I should screen-test for Mike, despite my reservations. I told my castmates in “Eh?” not to worry; I was sure they wouldn’t need to replace me. Then I walked to my neighbor on Eleventh Street, Mel Brooks, who’d suggested that I play a small part in “The Producers.” I called up to his window: “They’re flying me out to audition for a Mike Nichols movie.”

“Good luck!” he said, suppressing a laugh. “Keep me posted!”

I had to learn ten pages in less than forty-eight hours. I stayed up the entire night running lines; by the time I landed in Los Angeles, I hadn’t slept in two days. Mike’s office was a series of palatial rooms with high ceilings, and in my memory it included a bar, which is where I first saw him. “Oh, hi, would you like a drink?” he said. He was always so casual, almost seductive. Then they brought in Katharine Ross, who was outrageously beautiful. I felt foolish, like I had to apologize to her for looking like I did.

They took us to get our makeup done in a long room with rows of upholstered chairs. Today, you get made up in a trailer, without a trace of glamour, but this room was a remnant of Old Hollywood. It seemed likely that Betty Grable’s ass had been on the chair before mine.

They had these famous makeup artists, the Westmores—six brothers who’d learned their trade from their father. I can’t remember how many of them were there that day, but they were at it for hours. And it’s not like I was getting prosthetics or a toupee. It took them that long just to do something with what little I offered.

Mike came in, watched them for a while, and looked at my face in the mirror. Quietly, in his singsong voice, he said, “Can’t you do something with his eyebrows?” Bobby Duvall always said that I had only one. They started plucking me to make two.

Then Mike said that my neck looked too thick, so they put me in a turtleneck. But he was still unhappy with what he was seeing. (I, too, was increasingly unhappy.) Mike sounded almost innocent when he asked the Westmores, “Now, what are we going to do about the nose?”

I remember thinking, They’re trying to take the Jew off my face, and it ain’t going to happen. All I wanted to do was go home, to ethnic New York, where I belonged. I knew I was no leading man. I knew my place.

The scene I did with Katharine was endless. Both of us kept screwing up because—for God knows what reason—Mike wanted to shoot a ten-minute scene in one take. At one point, he took me aside and said, “Why are you nervous? This isn’t a play; the curtain’s not opening. It’s not a movie. It won’t go any farther than this room. So just relax!” I felt that he understood completely, and I thanked him and shook his hand. It was so slippery with sweat that it literally slid out of mine. That’s when I realized that he was more anxious than I was, and this did not put me at ease.

It wasn’t just paranoia: everyone thought I was wrong for the part. “I looked at it, and it was just this ugly boy playing the part, and I thought, Ugh,” the film’s editor, Sam O’Steen, later said of my screen test. People imagined the Braddocks as prototypical California gentiles. “All blonde, all healthy,” Buck Henry said. “A family of surfboards is what we called them. And here comes Dustin: clearly not a surfboard.” To save the film, they hoped Benjamin’s parents might be played by Ronald Reagan and Doris Day. “We immediately rationalized it: he’s a genetic throwback,” Buck continued. “Doris Day and Ronald Reagan have had this mutt .”

I was so relieved when we finished the screen test. I couldn’t wait to get out of there. As I was thanking the propman, a few subway tokens dropped out of my pocket. He very nicely picked them up, then said, “Here, kid, you’re gonna need these.”

Soon after I got home to New York, my agent told me to call Mike at nine o’clock on Sunday morning. It was snowing out, and I was going uptown to my girlfriend’s apartment for breakfast. Obviously, the agent meant Pacific time, but I was such an anxious wreck that I didn’t think it through. When I got to my girlfriend’s place, I called Mike at precisely 9 A.M. New York time and woke him up.

I mumbled an apology. There was a long silence. “Well,” Mike said, “you got it.”

Stunned is too weak a word. Mike had apparently seen something in the footage. “He had this thing I’d only seen in Elizabeth Taylor, and that I’d certainly not seen in any of the other tests,” he later told his biographer, Mark Harris. “That secret. That deal with Technicolor where you do nothing and it turns out you were doing everything. He was compelling and hilarious and impassive. It was startling. That’s what a great movie actor does. They don’t know how they do it, and I don’t know how they do it, but the difference is shocking.”

I hung up the phone feeling like I’d been hit in the head. I looked at my girlfriend, who was holding a spatula, making our breakfast. “I got it,” I told her.

We had three weeks of rehearsal, which was unheard of for a film—a testament to just how revered Mike was, how much leverage he had in the industry.

“Don’t try to do a character, don’t try to be funny,” he told us. “Start from zero.” Mike took me back to my adolescence—my acne, my barely suppressed horniness. He asked me if I thought Benjamin Braddock was a virgin. I said no, but that I didn’t think he’d ever screwed his mother’s friend before, either. (He liked that response.)

items.title: Iran, Khamenei avverte Trump: 'Se ci attaccate risposta senza confini'
items.summary: Secondo i media Usa, il tycoon vuole riprendere la guerra il giorno dopo le midterm
items.content:
Gli Stati Uniti hanno già allertato i Paesi del Golfo: una nuova offensiva contro l'Iran è possibile dopo le elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre. L'avvertimento risuona anche a Teheran, sulla quale da settimane aleggia lo spettro di nuovi raid. "Risponderemo a qualsiasi minaccia senza restrizioni geografiche", assicura la Guida suprema Mojtaba Khamenei in un incontro - ancora in una località segreta - con i vertici delle sue forze armate, lasciando intendere che il conflitto potrebbe estendersi al Golfo e oltre. Mentre i mediatori cercano di raggiungere un accordo che faccia ripartire le trattative e scongiuri un attacco in grado di mettere in pericolo i Paesi vicini dell'Iran, Donald Trump valuta le sue prossime mosse.

"Non ha ancora deciso. Siamo aperti a una soluzione diplomatica del conflitto", ha detto il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio da Atlanta, dove ha ospitato il G20 dei ministri degli Esteri, cercando di stemperare i timori di un attacco imminente. Rassicurazioni che, però, non convincono. Secondo indiscrezioni, infatti, il commander-in-chief sarebbe pronto a riprendere gli attacchi in caso di una sonora sconfitta dei repubblicani alle midterm. "Se si sentirà imbarazzato farà qualcosa di audace. E' questo che tutti dicono agli iraniani. Il momento migliore per arrivare a un accordo è ora", ha spiegato una fonte americana ad Axios. Un attacco potrebbe scattare dunque già il 4 novembre, all'indomani del voto, se i conservatori perdessero: procedere immediatamente consentirebbe a Trump di distogliere l'attenzione da una bruciante sconfitta e rivendicare il suo ruolo di leader di fronte ai democratici. L'amministrazione è comunque divisa su come procedere anche alla luce degli ingenti costi dell'operazione: solo i danni causati dagli attacchi iraniani alle strutture militari americani in Medio Oriente potrebbero raggiungere i 15 miliardi di dollari, che vanno sommati agli oltre 47 che la guerra è costata finora. Rubio e il capo del Pentagono Pete Hegsteh sono scettici sul raggiungimento di un accordo con l'attuale regime, mentre JD Vance e gli inviati Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner vogliono riprendere i negoziati.

items.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
items.summary: YouTube-style UI over 6,454 videos sourced from 39,834 HN comments since 2007. https://hackertube.org/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50319510 Points: 990 # Comments: 306
items.content:
It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org !

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews , filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

items.title: Rush finale alle midterm, Trump teme l'ondata dem
items.summary: Chiude la campagna in calo nei sondaggi. In Michigan lite fra i liberal, trema El-Sayed
items.content:
Il giorno della verità per Donald Trump e i repubblicani si avvicina, e l'ansia per un risultato deludente aumenta. I conservatori si preparano al peggio, temendo di essere travolti alla Camera e di perdere anche il Senato. Nonostante il calo nei sondaggi - il suo tasso di gradimento è sceso al 37% - , il presidente continua a ostentare sicurezza pubblicamente, ma il suo umore dietro le quinte si sta incupendo di giorno in giorno. Per mantenere la Camera serve un "miracolo" mentre al Senato i conservatori ce la possono ancora fare, nonostante alcune corse "preoccupano", ha ammesso Steve Bannon, l'ex controverso stratega della Casa Bianca, convinto che all'indomani del voto scoppierà una "guerra civile" all'interno del partito. Non mancano grane neanche in casa dei democratici. Dopo lo scandalo di omonimia in Alaska, a tremare è anche il Michigan con il duro botta e risposta fra il candidato al Senato Abdul El-Sayed e Haley Stevens, battuta alle primarie nei mesi scorsi. Stevens ha chiesto al candidato di prendere le distanze da uno spot critico degli aiuti degli Stati Uniti a Israele, finanziato da un pac di sinistra. El-Sayed non solo si è rifiutato: l'ha attaccata parlando di una vendetta per la sconfitta subita e l'ha esortata a tenersi alla larga della sua campagna in questi ultimi giorni prima del voto. Il braccio di ferro ha fatto saltare la loro attesa apparizione congiunta che aveva come obiettivo quello di mostrare l'unità delle due anime del partito, la progressista e la moderata, alla vigilia del voto. Lo scontro invece ha rivelato le difficoltà dei democratici con il rischio di danneggiare El-Sayed, già nel mirino di Trump e dei repubblicani per la sua fede musulmana. "E' un rischio per la sicurezza nazionale", denuncia quasi quotidianamente il suo rivale repubblicano Mike Rogers.

"E' un jihadista", tuona a ogni comizio il presidente. Il Michigan è uno degli Stati che decideranno gli equilibri del potere in Senato. Se El-Sayed e James Talarico, il candidato democratico al Senato in Texas, sono i suoi bersagli preferiti, Trump da giorni non perde occasione di ricordare quanto sta accadendo in Alaska con i due Dan Sullivan al voto. "E' frode elettorale", ripete come un mantra puntando il dito contro i democratici che hanno cercato un omonimo del candidato repubblicano per sottrargli voti. Al momento il Sullivan scovato dai liberal non è chiaro dove sia: ha lasciato la sua abitazione e l'ultima volta che è stato visto in pubblico - riporta Cbs - è stato su un volo per Anchorage. Le critiche del presidente non risparmiano neanche la giustizia della California, Stato che ha definito più volte corrotto.

"Continueremo a batterci per l'integrità delle elezioni", ha assicurato dopo che una corte d'appello federale ha respinto la richiesta del Dipartimento di Giustizia di ordinare alla California di accantonare 20.000 voti di presunti elettori non cittadini americani. Sulla stessa scia la decisione di un altro giudice che, in un provvedimento temporaneo, ha bloccato le varie tattiche adottate dell'amministrazione Trump per fare pressione sui funzionari elettorali. I tentativi del presidente di insinuare dubbi sul voto preoccupano i democratici e li spingono a correre ai ripari. Allarmati da come il tycoon potrebbe reagire di fronte a una sconfitta, i liberal hanno deciso di allestire una 'war room' per il giorno dopo le elezioni per fermare gli sforzi del presidente di "rubare le elezioni", ha spiegato il leader dei democratici in Senato Chuck Schumer, che è al lavoro con una squadra di legali per mettere a punto la strategia da seguire. Uno dei rischi maggiori è quello che l'amministrazione tenti di bloccare la certificazione del voto da parte degli Stati. In Alaska, altro Stato chiave per la conquista del Senato, il Dipartimento di Giustizia ha già chiesto preventivamente di non procede qualora il Sullivan repubblicano perdesse, e il governatore non ha escluso di impedire il conteggio. Mentre le cause procedono, Trump chiuderà la campagna elettorale in Iowa e in Kansas, lanciando il suo ultimo appello agli elettori a votare: "Se vincono i democratici avrete una depressione economica, se vinciamo noi avrete in tasca 5.000 dollari".

items.title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
items.summary: One evacuated couple says they crossed minefields in Oleshky in search of food.
items.content:
Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".

Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."

The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.

Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.

Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.

As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.

Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.

"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.

That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.

Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.

Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.

On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers.

As Mykhailo Palii arrived, his daughters Dasha and Anya, who thought they might never see him again, sprinted across the tarmac screaming and crying.

After an emotional embrace, Palii described a glimpse of life in Oleshky, although he said he had, until then, kept many of the details from his family.

"A hole was blown into the bathroom," he said. "There were drone attacks and missile strikes. It happened, but I didn't tell them about it because I knew they would worry."

Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.

For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.

But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.

Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.

Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."

Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.

Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city

Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire

Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
