items.title: The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
items.summary: Indian chef Ranji Smile opened America’s first Indian restaurant in 1901 - then became a fake prince.
items.content:
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US.

Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene.

In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name.

"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail".

Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe.

Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue.

In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah.

Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff.

At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback.

Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon".

Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him."

As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier , external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome.

Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns.

As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans.

Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad.

Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flair for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity.

Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants".

All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported.

"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof.

Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country.

In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility.

While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him.

Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant.

The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear.

Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters.

In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo".

Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf).

Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island.

Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit.

New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America.

That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.

Dinyar Patel is associate professor of history at SPJIMR in Mumbai

items.title: Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis
items.summary: Filter straws to a disposable toilet - people in the US, Japan, Sweden and Netherlands on what's in their emergency stashes.
items.content:
Sales of tinned food, radios and torches spiked in some shops after the UK government advised households what to stock up on in case of a national emergency.

While having this stash - or personal crisis kit - is new to the UK, it's common in many places across the world.

Countries facing extreme weather, natural disasters and fraught geopolitical situations regularly issue preparedness guidance - some even delivering booklets directly to homes.

So what do these emergency supplies look like for some and how do they manage it?

Thirty-year-old Andreas Wennerberg had never really thought about preparing for emergencies, until a government booklet arrived through his door two years ago.

Posted to every household in Sweden, it detailed what to stock up on and how to act "in case of crisis or war".

Andreas, who lives in Stockholm, built up a relatively small stockpile in his basement, including a crank radio, a tank with 10 litres of water and about 2,230 SEK (£170) in cash. He says he already owned some of the items.

It was a "wake-up call", he says, but admits he hasn't followed the guidance in full.

Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.

"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.

In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency , external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.

Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".

Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat.

But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.

Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide , external , which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.

In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers.

"A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.

Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.

Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.

The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.

As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.

To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.

Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.

The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.

Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.

He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.

Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire.

"Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."

In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.

At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".

Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."

Do you have a personal crisis kit where you live in the world?

Do you have a personal crisis kit where you live in the world?

Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water

items.title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
items.summary: Countries have been trying to get a global agreement to halt nature decline back on track.
items.content:
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.

The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.

Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.

"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.

Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.

That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.

The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.

But according to the UN this week, , external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.

As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.

"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.

"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.

This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."

But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".

Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection , external - an area bigger than Greenland.

Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.

Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.

In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.

But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , external

At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.

Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment.

"A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."

Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice.

"So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."

A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually - at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.

Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged.

"When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."

One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature.

But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process.

"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency.

Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding.

"This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

items.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
items.summary: The escalation came after the government suspended two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.
items.content:
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.

The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).

The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.

Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.

President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.

Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.

Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.

In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.

"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."

The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.

Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.

One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.

Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.

Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.

Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.

Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.

But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.

Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".

"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.

"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

Poland's conservative president-elect to be tough opponent for PM

items.title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
items.summary: From Alaska to Texas, candidates with an eye on Congress are using their personal style to stand out.
items.content:
As Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.

In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal.

"Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.

From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.

Some candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.

The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022.

She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.

Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from".

"Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.

Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.

Democratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.

She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.

During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.

The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.

Other candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.

While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.

In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.

She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June.

The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard.

"Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says.

"It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."

Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial.

"Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."

Once a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.

On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.

"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway.

"The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."

Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas".

"Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations.

"Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."

Meanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front.

It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".

The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms.

"The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising.

"A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit.

"The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.

A uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.

It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.

Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns.

Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator.

"Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."

"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.

Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.

The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics".

The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.

It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says.

"The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."

Friedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump.

His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House.

"[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says.

"If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.

Whatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in.

"What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians

items.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
items.summary: Thailand has prosecuted 294 people since 2020 under its lèse majesté law, with sentences going up to 50 years.
items.content:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.

The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.

One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.

This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.

"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.

Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".

Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."

In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.

"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."

From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.

"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."

Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.

Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.

But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.

The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.

That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.

In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.

In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.

At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.

But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.

One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.

She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.

A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.

She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.

"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.

"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."

In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.

"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."

Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.

She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.

"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."

She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.

Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.

Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.

But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.

items.title: Tecla Bossi: “Anch’io scesi in piazza per Giulia Cecchettin. Elena? Spero di renderle giustizia”
items.summary: In ‘Se domani non torno’ Tecla Bossi interpreta Elena Cecchettin, sorella di Giulia: “Non per farne un’eroina, ma per mostrare una normalità completamente sconvolta”
items.content:
“Anch’io sono scesa in piazza per Giulia Cecchettin. Elena è diventata un simbolo, ma senza volerlo. Ci siamo incontrate e conosciute, mi sembrava un segno di rispetto. Spero di rendere giustizia a lei e alla sua famiglia”. Tecla Bossi, 26 anni , al suo esordio al cinema nel film Se domani non torno , diretto da Paola Randi (in sala dal 5 novembre), interpreta la sorella della studentessa di Vigonovo, Venezia, uccisa a 22 anni dall’ex compagno Filippo Turetta. Un femminicidio che ha scosso l’Italia, riacceso il dibattito sulla violenza di genere e il patriarcato, e che ha portato migliaia di giovani a scendere in strada e manifestare. Tra loro, c’era anche Tecla.

“Ricordo che in quel periodo mi ero da poco trasferita a Venezia per frequentare l’accademia di recitazione. Sono andata alle manifestazioni per lei con i miei compagni, impossibile ignorare quello che era successo. Ero già scesa in piazza, prima, ma in quel caso ho sentito una partecipazione molto più grande, ho incontrato persone che mai avrei immaginato di vedere: è stato incredibile. Poi ho sentito parlare Elena e suo papà Gino…”.

E oggi lei interpreta proprio Elena, che con le sue parole per la sorella diventò subito un simbolo. Citando una poesia, scandì: “Per Giulia non fate rumore, per Giulia bruciate tutto”.

“Non mi permetto di parlare per Elena. Ma penso che la cosa più importante da ricordare è che lei si è ritrovata in questa situazione, a vivere questo trauma, senza volerlo. Nel cercare di reagire, ha sentito la necessità di parlare, di mettere le cose in chiaro, e tutto questo ha scatenato conseguenze, tra cui diventare un simbolo. Senza volerlo, appunto. È stato un peso in più”.

“È stato difficile gestire il peso emotivo del personaggio. Parliamo di una persona che ha la mia età, la sua vita. Non volevo fare qualcosa che potesse non rappresentarla in modo corretto. Il nostro lavoro è stato quello di incanalare al meglio le emozioni per non farne una copia o un’imitazione. Ho letto le sue interviste, ascoltato i suoi interventi, studiato come parla e si muove. Mi sono sforzata di calibrare ogni volta la fragilità, la rabbia. Per non farne un’eroina – si è parlato di lei anche così – ma parte di una normalità completamente sconvolta”.

“Ci siamo incontrate e confrontate, quasi come due ragazze, due amiche. Era un modo per dirle: sono io che faccio te, mi sembrava un gesto di rispetto. Ho conosciuto anche Gino, che è venuto sul set diverse volte”.

“Mi sono riconosciuta molto nel contesto. Siamo coetanee, entrambe primogenite, abbiamo lo stesso background culturale, secondo me abbiamo avuto una quotidianità simile. Come persona non posso saperlo, ma come personaggio mi sono ritrovata molto in alcune parti che abbiamo girato, legate a momenti di fragilità”.

“Spero in primo luogo di rendere giustizia a Elena e alla sua famiglia. La cosa più importante, quando si fanno questi lavori e ci sono persone vive coinvolte, è avere rispetto, cura, delicatezza. Portare una storia già molto nota al cinema vuol dire amplificare alcuni aspetti per continuare a sviluppare un dialogo sulla parità di genere, soprattutto per le nuove generazioni. I ragazzi e le ragazze sono già consapevoli, ma serve che siano seguiti, guidati. Spero che questo film possa essere una parte di questo percorso”.

“Spero che lo vedano più persone possibili. C’è una cosa che, tra le altre, mi commuove. Riguarda Gino Cecchettin, che si rende conto di non sapere nulla del patriarcato, ha sempre pensato che non lo riguardasse. Dopo il femminicidio si mette in discussione, fa una rivoluzione su se stesso, chiede a Elena una mano. È commovente che un adulto, uomo, maschio, lo abbia fatto. Io non ho la pretesa che questo film cambi il mondo, ma se anche soltanto qualcuno ci farà un pensiero sarà bellissimo”.

“Io sono sempre stata sensibile. Non mi sono mai ritenuta un’attivista o una militante, ma una persona che cerca di tenersi informata il più possibile, che prova a mettere in pratica comportamenti femministi, per cambiare le cose. Recitare in questo film mi ha fatto fare una rilfessioni in più, un confronto più forte con me stessa. Mi sono chiesta: io cosa posso fare? E mi sono data una risposta: più di quanto credessi”.

items.title: In alto l’antenna. Intervista a Neil Harbisson, il primo cyborg riconosciuto al mondo
items.summary: L’artista-attivista ha un sensore integrato sulla testa con cui non solo è riuscito a vedere, ma anche a sognare raggi ultravioletti e infrarossi. E ha nuove idee per farci percepire il futuro
items.content:
“Il rischio non è diventare meno umani, ma perdere la libertà di decidere se continuare a esserlo”. È il confine esplorato da Neil Harbisson: artista, filosofo e attivista britannico-spagnolo a cui è stato ufficialmente riconosciuto lo status di cyborg, primo al mondo e nella storia. Nato con l’acromatopsia, o visione monocromatica (patologia ereditaria rara che influisce sulla percezione dei colori), nel 2004 ha iniziato a utilizzare un’antenna impiantata nel cranio capace di trasformare le frequenze cromatiche in suoni. Deciso a esplorare le potenzialità della tecnologia applicate alla sensorialità, ha creato la Cyborg Foundation per portare nel mondo le sue ricerche. Come ha fatto in Italia, ospite al Festival Là Fuori di Roma e poi all’Over The Real International Video & Multimedia Art Festival di Lucca.

Per lei che cosa significa essere ufficialmente una persona cyborg?

“Semplicemente definisce il fatto che esista una tecnologia integrata, nel corpo o nella mente, che è diventata parte della mia identità. Non si tratta di un dispositivo accessorio o esterno a me: è diventato parte del modo in cui riesco a percepire la realtà. Quando ho iniziato a usare l’antenna, volevo semplicemente riuscire a distinguere i colori. Poi ho scoperto di poter sentire frequenze che normalmente gli esseri umani non avvertono, ultravioletti e infrarossi. Così quel limite è diventato opportunità per sviluppare un nuovo senso”.

“Rileva la frequenza della luce e la converte in vibrazioni sonore che poi vengono trasmesse attraverso il cranio. Ogni colore corrisponde a frequenze diverse. All’inizio dovevo interpretare i suoni, dopo anni il mio cervello ha iniziato a elaborarli come informazioni percettive. Ora riesco persino a sognare a colori”.

Lei sta lavorando anche sulla percezione del tempo, su come “sentirlo”. Che significa?

“Non tanto per sapere che ore sono, per quello abbiamo gli orologi, ma creare illusioni temporali, al pari di quelle ottiche che ingannano la vista. Così ho elaborato il dispositivo Solar Crown, che sfrutta il calore del corpo per compiere un giro attorno alla testa in 24 ore: variando la velocità, riesco a creare sensazioni diverse in base allo scorrere del tempo”.

“È una forma di libertà, permette di sperimentare prima ancora di sapere cosa sia qualcosa. La scienza si chiede se una cosa sia possibile, l’arte ci prova”.

Quando il corpo diventa uno spazio di sperimentazione, entrano in gioco i diritti. Cosa manca ancora al riconoscimento dell’identità cyborg?

“Il diritto di modificare volontariamente il nostro corpo, accedere alla tecnologia che diventa parte di noi e proteggere i dati generati dai nostri sensi e impianti. Se una tecnologia diventa parte integrante della nostra fisicità, non va trattata come un dispositivo esterno”.

Un concetto che rende quasi naturale il passaggio successivo: lei considera l’intelligenza artificiale un’estensione della mente o della sensorialità?

“Un nuovo senso cambia il modo in cui percepisci il mondo, l’Ai cambia il tuo, come crei o comunichi. Entrambi mettono in discussione il confine tra biologico e tecnologico”.

Ma che cosa succederebbe se un prodotto della tecnologia, creato da esseri umani, manifestasse volontà propria? Le è mai successo di provare una simile “dissociazione” rispetto alla sua antenna?

“In realtà si tratta di una convivenza che sto ancora cercando di comprendere. A volte ci ho anche litigato, ma è un’ottima coinquilina: ha la sua stanza e il suo tavolo. Il suo modo di ragionare sembra esprimere una vita propria. Mi interroga sulla mia esistenza di cyborg. È diventato un esperimento filosofico, non più solo tecnologico”.

Se in un prossimo futuro potessimo scegliere quali sensi modificare o privilegiare, come cambiare i nostri corpi o formulare nuove idee attraverso l’Ai, ci potremo ancora definire “umani”?

“Come individui credo senz’altro di sì, ma l’umanità sarebbe meno definita dal punto di vista biologico. Credo che impianti come il mio saranno sempre più comuni e il cambiamento più significativo sarà psicologico: avvertiamo la tecnologia come parte di ciò che siamo. Quando inizieremo a progettare i nostri sensi e scegliere come percepire la realtà, l’idea di una fisicità immutabile sarà difficile da sostenere. Ma se aziende o governi dovessero controllare impianti o Ai, le tecnologie nate per espandere le nostre capacità rischiano di diventare strumenti di controllo”.

items.title: Sienna Miller: “Divorziare è terribile: due persone che si amavano finiscono per odiarsi”
items.summary: Nella prossima serie tv mette in scena la fine burrascosa di un matrimonio. Ma Sienna Miller crede nell’amore e sogna un giorno di diventare Giulietta, purché Romeo...
items.content:
Sienna Rose Diana Miller , newyorkese di nascita ma cresciuta a Londra, per anni è stata l’“it girl” anticonformista per eccellenza, ultra-scrutinata dai tabloid e dal gossip hollywodiano, pluripremiata e tre volte madre, accompagnata sempre da uno spirito ribelle e da una grande curiosità. Per il mondo del cinema sappiamo che è letteralmente esplosa grazie ad Alfie, seguito da Factory Girl, poi la sua carriera ebbe una svolta con due film candidati all’Oscar: Foxcatcher , diretto da Bennett Miller, e American Sniper , di Clint Eastwood. Ora, alla vigilia dei 45 anni, la ritroviamo nel serial drama a sfondo legale War. Il divorzio del secolo – produzione Sky Original, dal 27 novembre su Sky e Now – dove Sienna (incinta del suo terzo figlio durante le riprese) interpreta un’attrice di successo coinvolta in un divorzio di grande risonanza. Il marito, Dominic West, è un ricco magnate britannico delle tecnologie. I due ingaggiano studi legali rivali per contendersi denaro, case, opere d’arte, beni e persino il figlio di lei. Le chiediamo se ogni similitudine con le sue separazioni – da Jude Law e Tom Sturridge, se non sapete già tutto di questi due casi basta chiedere a Google – sia puramente casuale.

Di certo, signora Miller, le avrà fatto passare la voglia di divorziare di nuovo.

“Assolutamente sì! Non andrei mai in tribunale, coinvolgere grandi avvocati in un divorzio non fa altro che trasformare un conflitto personale in una costosa battaglia senza fine. La cosa interessante da chiedersi è come sia possibile che due persone che si amavano possano finire per odiarsi in quel modo estremo. Il dramma è proprio quella linea sottile tra amore e odio”.

“Solo una scena è ispirata a fatti realmente accaduti, quando l’attrice e regista Olivia Wilde ha ricevuto i documenti per l’affido dei figli da parte di Jason Sudeikis direttamente sul palco del CinemaCon a Las Vegas, mentre presentava il suo film Don’t Worry Darling, gesto che personalmente ho trovato orribile. Più approfondisci il mondo dei divorzi di alto profilo, più ti rendi conto che sono pieni di drammi: accordi prematrimoniali, relazioni extraconiugali, beni immobili, figli. Ho sempre adorato la tv dei legal drama, Ally McBeal, The Good Wife e The West Wing, alcuni di quei momenti sono stati fonte di ispirazione per la nostra serie”.

L’ultima volta che aveva lavorato con Dominic West risale a 21 anni fa, a teatro.

“Era nel West End, la commedia di Shakespeare Come vi piace. È stato il mio primo spettacolo teatrale, e quando reciti in cento repliche, finisci per conoscerti bene davvero. Essere amici nella vita privata ha influenzato molto la nostra relazione sul set, direi che è stato essenziale per inscenare la relazione conflittuale di un matrimonio. Trovo divertente essere cattivi per finta, magari proprio con le persone a cui vuoi bene. E dovevamo avere quel tipo di disinvoltura reciproca che si crea in queste situazioni”.

“È una persona impulsiva, non reagisce bene quando la mettono sotto pressione. Penso di avere anche io queste caratteristiche, anche se non sono così spietata. Mi piace però che voglia difendere la propria reputazione e cercare di rimanere professionale, riuscendo a nascondere ciò che pensa davvero della posizione di Morgan, dei suoi principi morali. Sa gestire le proprie emozioni”.

È stato difficile conciliare la sua maternità con una tabella di marcia lavorativa così intensa?

“È impegnativo, passare tre mesi sul set richiede una buona organizzazione, ed è l’irregolarità a rendere tutto più complicato. È un lavoro di alti e bassi, pieni e vuoti, a volte ho tanto tempo da dedicare ai miei figli, altre volte li vedo pochissimo. Trovare il giusto equilibrio è sempre un dilemma, soddisfare le proprie esigenze creative ed essere allo stesso tempo presente per loro, senza sentirsi in colpa, è una costante di questo mestiere”.

“Assolutamente sì, ho altre priorità rispetto alle mie esigenze personali, non sono mai stata neanche troppo ambiziosa. Penso che per avere successo bisogna essere un po’ più determinati e strategici di quanto lo sia io. Devi scendere a compromessi dal punto di vista artistico, e io non sono mai stata particolarmente brava a farlo”.

All’inizio della carriera era la fidanzata di un attore già famoso (Jude Law, ndr). È stato difficile essere presa sul serio come attrice?

“Molto. La gente faceva supposizioni su di me, senza conoscere il mio lavoro o avermi mai vista in un film. Molti mi hanno augurato di fallire. Fortunatamente ho avuto modo di mettermi alla prova nei panni di Edie Sedgwick, la musa di Warhol in Factory Girl: è stata la prima volta in cui ho capito che recitare era davvero ciò che dovevo fare”.

“Le cose sono diverse, il calibro dei registi e degli attori con cui ho lavorato ha cambiato il corso della mia carriera. Sono cambiata anche io: più motivata, concentrata e più esigente di prima. Soprattutto, ho rivalutato il tipo di cinema a cui voglio dedicarmi”.

“Continuo a volere ruoli profondi, tipo Giulietta. Ne ho parlato anche recentemente con un regista teatrale molto famoso, si è messo a ridere, anche se non voleva prendermi in giro, dicendomi che il pubblico farebbe fatica a vedermi come una vergine! Io però ci credo ancora, ho solo bisogno di un Romeo più anziano, non trova?”.

“Era il mio sogno fin da quando ero molto piccola, mia madre gestiva una scuola di recitazione. Spesso andavamo a teatro o a vedere qualche balletto. Ricordo uno spettacolo interpretato da Richard Burton intitolato Anna dei mille giorni, sulla storia di Anna Bolena: quanto erano belli, ne ero ossessionata. Ho adorato Katharine Hepburn, Judi Dench, Clara Bow e tutte le star del cinema muto, compreso Chaplin. Amo il teatro perché è approfondimento, esperienza e ricerca”.

Quant’è importante il suo impegno nel campo della beneficenza?

“Sono Ambasciatrice globale dell’International Medical Corps, ho visitato regioni colpite da crisi umanitarie: Haiti, Etiopia, Libano, Giordania, Sud Sudan e la Repubblica Democratica del Congo, dove ho visto gli orrori della guerra. Trovo importante questo tipo di volontariato, che si concentra sull’emancipazione delle comunità locali, dignità e autosufficienza a lungo termine, piuttosto che su soluzioni temporanee. Uso il piccolo potere dei social media per sensibilizzare l’opinione pubblica sui soccorsi di emergenza, sulle cliniche e sui servizi di salute mentale forniti dai soccorritori di Imc”.

“Adoro cucinare. Ho un piccolo cottage in campagna dove coltivo un orto. Sto lavorando ad avere una casa autosufficiente, con pannelli solari per l’energia sostenibile. Lì trovo l’equilibrio, lontano dalla frenesia. Mi piace passare del tempo con gli amici o la famiglia, facendo cose normali. Amo stare intorno a un tavolo, con un buon roast beef all’inglese e fare una piacevole conversazione”.
